title: You are handed an impossible deadline
lede: "We need this by Friday." It is Wednesday afternoon. The work is realistically eight days. Everyone in the room nods, and the nodding is doing a lot of work.

blocks.text: "We need this by Friday." It is Wednesday afternoon. The work is realistically eight days. Everyone in the room nods, and the nodding is doing a lot of work.

items: Saying yes to an impossible date is not commitment, it is a deferred and larger failure. You are trading four days of approval for a Friday where you deliver something broken and own it alone.

The word "no" is usually not available to you and usually is not necessary. What is available is making the trade-off visible, so the decision about what gets sacrificed is made by the person with the authority to make it.
People asking for impossible dates are often not lying — they frequently have no model of what the work contains. Your job is to supply the model, quickly and without drama.

items.detail: Ask for an hour. Instant yes is a promise you cannot price; instant no is a fight you do not need.

items.move: Break the work into named parts with hours
items.detail: Rough is fine. A list of six items with estimates converts your feeling into an argument someone else can check.
Full scope later, reduced scope Friday, full scope Friday with named help. Three doors invite a decision; one wall invites a fight.

items.move: Make the sacrifice explicit and get it acknowledged
items.detail: Whatever gets dropped, say its name and get a yes in writing. "We deprioritised testing" must be their sentence, not your excuse later.

items.move: Confirm in writing, briefly, same day
items.detail: One short message: what you will deliver, what you will not, what you assumed. This is the entire defence for what happens on Friday.

items.say: "Let me look at what's in it and come back within the hour with what Friday can actually contain."
"Friday is possible for A and B. C needs another week, or it ships without testing. Which do you want?"
"Friday works if someone takes the data migration. Without that, Tuesday."
"To confirm: Friday, A and B only, C moves to the 20th, and we accepted lighter QA on B."

items: Heroic silence, then working the weekend to hide the gap. It teaches everyone that impossible dates work.
The vague "I'll try." It reads as yes to them and as no to you, which is how people end up furious with each other.
Making it emotional — "I'm already drowning." True, and less effective than six line items with hours.
Renegotiating on Thursday night. Trade-offs are cheap on Wednesday and expensive at the deadline.
Refusing without offering a route. That is how competent people get labelled obstructive.
Keep the estimate you made and compare it to reality. Two or three rounds of this makes you the person whose dates are believed, which is quiet power.
If impossible dates are constant, the problem is capacity or planning, not your speed. Raise it as a pattern, with your data, in a calm moment.
Notice if the sacrifice you named gets remembered as your failure. If so, put the trade-off in writing at the point of decision from now on.
